pr_title: Build a NuGet Package for ConPTY
pr_body:
This pull request introduces a packaging phase that emits
Microsoft.Windows.Console.ConPTY, a nuget package that contains the
pseudoconsole API as well as the requisite copies of conhost.

* winconpty learned to load a version of OpenConsole.exe specific to the
  processor architecture on its hosting machine
* the package, as well as its contents, is signed properly and is nearly
  ready for distribution via nuget.org
* the API in conpty-static.h has been adjusted to expose
  CreatePseudoConsoleAsUser and stamp out the correct DLL import/export
  annotations.
* getting .NET to play right was somewhat challenging, but I tested this
  against .NET 6.0 and it seemed to work properly; it shipped conpty.dll
  in the right places, and it shipped OpenConsole.exe next to the
  published application.

In the future, we could provide an interop assembly for C# consumers;
that is, unfortunately, out of scope today.

Closes #3577
Closes #3568
Obsoletes #1130
pr_comments:
Doing a "fully loaded" build here: https://microsoft.visualstudio.com/Dart/_build/results?buildId=48515923&view=results

We'll see if it pans out!

I was worried that the extra link step for `OpenConsole.exe` would introduce "torn symbols", where the version in the package could not be debugged because it didn't have a file hash that matched the PDB. I tested this, and the EXE file is _identical_. WinDbg did not complain about it at all, and loaded the right symbols.

issue_context.title: conpty: produce a NuGet package (for internal consumption, for now)
issue_context.body:
* [x] #3568 make sure all three conhosts are inside it


see also: #1130

review_comments:
Shouldn't this be `L"\\OpenConsole.exe"`?
Also: Should we wrap this code in a feature check? It seems very specific to our nuget version...

filesystem::path::append does the right thing here.

In addition, this logic (1) starts with and (2) falls back to, the original code. If you were using conpty.dll before (which you should not have been, as it was not being distributed!) it will still look for OpenConsole.exe in the same folder *first*, and it will still fall back to conhost *last*.

There is no feature flag that will allow us to build this code differently based on whether it is inside the nuget package or not, and I would rather not introduce that complexity.

Now that I am at a full non-phone keyboard, here's why I think it would add complexity.

Right now, our feature flags support *branding* and *branches*. A Branding is pretty much which store package we're building, or "windows inbox" for conhost. That's another way to "brand" our codebase. Branches are branches obviously :D

Brandings are *mutually exclusive*. You can't activate two brandings at once. They're supposed to represent a single unified product flow, from Dev->Preview->Stable.

Introducing feature flags for _the conpty package_ within that existing infrastructure requires us to add a new branding. "This is the terminal repo, built for ConPTY_Package". However, we lose a bunch of flexibility here:

1. We would not be able to produce a build with the same code, that is, OpenConsole.exe and winconpty.lib, as a Terminal release or a WPF control release
2. We would not be able to have "Preview" conpty features (unless we added a second new branding, ConPTY_Package_Preview.)
3. We would need to compile the code three *more* times per build to activate that branding on only the components that it matters for. Right now, our build matrix is "[Win10, Win11] * [x86, x64, arm64] * [Preview, Stable]". That's 12 builds on a good day. I don't want to add more.
And it wouldn't get us much. It would remove a middle-tier fallback to look for a right-architecture conpty host.
